summary: Common text with ITU Recommendation H.248 as redetermined in February 2000, defining the Megaco protocol for controlling media gateways. It is read together with RFC 2886. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 3015.

eli5.summary: A controller tells a media gateway how to connect phone calls. This was an early version of those control rules and was replaced.

subtitle: A protocol for controllers to manage decomposed media gateways over networks.

tldr.problem: Large multimedia systems need to split media gateway functions across multiple physical devices controlled from a central location, but they lack a standard way for controllers to manage these distributed gateways and their connections.
tldr.mechanism: Megaco defines a protocol where a Media Gateway Controller (MGC) sends commands to Media Gateways (MGs) to add, modify, remove or move terminations (connection endpoints), with events detected on terminations reported back to the controller, all organized into transactions sent over TCP or UDP.
tldr.outcome: The protocol enables flexible, distributed gateway architectures supporting diverse connection types (analog phone lines, digital trunks, IP streams) and signaling systems. This version was replaced by RFC 3015 as the protocol evolved.

today: RFC 2885 is Historic; it was replaced by RFC 3015, which defines Megaco Protocol version 1.0. This version 0.8 is the original protocol specification common with ITU-T H.248 from February 2000. Implementations should use RFC 3015 and later versions.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Megaco protocol (also known as H.248) is a framework for controlling media gateways in decomposed, distributed telephone systems. A traditional gateway is a single device that bridges circuit-switched phone networks (like ISDN or analog lines) with packet networks (like IP). Megaco allows that gateway to be split: the media processing lives on one or more media gateways, while the call control logic lives in a separate Media Gateway Controller (MGC). The MGC directs the MGs by sending commands to set up connections, apply tones and announcements, detect button presses and off-hook events, and gather statistics.

This document defines the common text with ITU Recommendation H.248 as fixed in February 2000. It meets the requirements for media gateway control documented in RFC 2805 and supports diverse signaling systems (ISDN, tone signaling, SS7, QSIG, GSM) and bearer interfaces (IP, ATM, others).
sections.eli5: Megaco is how a computer (the controller) tells a telephone switcher (the gateway) what to do with incoming phone calls: pick up a line, play a tone, listen for button presses, hang up when done.

sections.title: Connection Model: Contexts and Terminations
sections.content:
Megaco models a media gateway's controllable parts using two core abstractions: Terminations and Contexts.

A Termination is a logical entity that sources or sinks one or more media streams. It might represent a physical phone line (DS0 channel, analog interface), an RTP stream from the network, or a virtual connection. Each termination has properties grouped into descriptors: media parameters, detected events, applied signals (tones, announcements), and statistics.

A Context is an association of multiple Terminations, defining how they connect to each other: who hears or sees whom, any mixing or switching applied. A special null Context holds terminations not yet in active association. When the last termination is removed from a context, the context is deleted. Terminations are identified by TerminationIDs chosen by the gateway; a wildcard mechanism (ALL for multiple terminations, CHOOSE for gateway selection) allows bulk operations.

Different gateway types define optional properties through Packages—named sets of Properties, Events, Signals and Statistics. An MGC can audit a termination to discover which packages it implements, enabling interoperability despite diverse hardware.
sections.eli5: A termination is like a phone jack or a connection; a context is like a call connecting two or more jacks together. The gateway groups these so the controller can say things like 'connect jack 1 to jack 3' or 'detect when jack 2 goes off-hook'.

sections.title: Commands: Controlling Terminations and Contexts
sections.content:
The MGC controls the MG by issuing eight command types, each operating on terminations or contexts:

  • Add creates or adds a termination to a context. If no context exists yet, the Add command creates one. An Add can specify media parameters, events to detect, signals to apply, and digit maps.
  • Modify changes properties, events, and signals of an existing termination.
  • Subtract removes a termination from its context and returns statistics about the termination's participation. When the last termination leaves, the context is deleted.
  • Move atomically relocates a termination from one context to another in a single operation.
  • AuditValue queries the current values of termination properties, events, signals, and statistics. Wildcarding can audit multiple terminations at once, with union results suppressing duplicates.
  • AuditCapabilities returns the possible values and ranges a termination can support.
  • Notify is sent from the MG to the MGC to report detected events in order, with timestamps and parameters.
  • ServiceChange informs the MGC that a termination or group is being taken out of or returned to service, or announces gateway availability (registration), restart, or control handoff.

Parameters to commands are organized into Descriptors: Media descriptors specify streams and bearer properties; Modem descriptors define modem types; Events descriptors specify which events to detect and how to react; Signals descriptors apply tones and announcements; Digit Map descriptors set up dialing plans with timing; Statistics descriptors return call data. Most descriptors can be used as input (to set values) or output (to return chosen or current values).
sections.eli5: The controller sends eight types of orders: Add a connection, Modify settings, Subtract (disconnect), Move between connections, ask Audit what it is, Audit what it could do, listen for Notify messages, and send ServiceChange status. Each order includes labels saying what media, tones, or digit patterns to use.

sections.title: Transactions and Message Structure
sections.content:
Commands are bundled into Transactions, each identified by a TransactionID assigned by the sender and unique within that sender's scope. A transaction request contains one or more Actions, each scoped to a single Context and containing one or more Commands. The responder returns a TransactionReply with results for each command, or errors if any fail. A TransactionPending can be sent to indicate that processing continues, preventing the sender from timing out prematurely.

Multiple transactions are concatenated into a Message, which has a header with the sender's identity (Message Identifier, or MID) and a protocol version number. The MID is typically a domain address, domain name, or device name. Transactions within a message are treated independently; there is no ordering or message-level acknowledgement.

The protocol supports two encoding formats: binary (defined in Annex A using ASN.1) and text (defined in Annex B using ABNF). MGCs must support both; MGs may support one or both. The text encoding uses SDP (Session Description Protocol) for media and remote descriptors, while the binary encoding uses defined tags.
sections.eli5: Commands get bundled into transactions, each with an ID so the answer matches the question. Multiple transactions fit in one message, which has a sender's name and version number at the top.

sections.title: Transport and Protocol Operation
sections.content:
Messages are transported over either TCP or UDP, with the default ports being 2944 for text encoding and 2945 for binary encoding (for either protocol). For IP, MGCs must support both TCP and UDP/Application Level Framing (ALF); MGs must support at least one.

The MG is pre-provisioned with the address of a primary MGC and optionally secondary MGCs. Upon initial registration (cold start), the MG sends a ServiceChange command with the Restart method to its primary MGC. If the MGC responds with a different MGC ID, the MG contacts that controller instead. If all primary and secondary MGCs fail to respond, the MG waits a random interval (typically 600 seconds for residential gateways, shorter for trunk gateways) to prevent a restart avalanche when many gateways power up simultaneously.

The protocol does not mandate that the underlying transport guarantees command ordering, allowing parallel processing of commands on different terminations. However, commands on the same termination should normally be executed serially (except Subtract, which can be issued anytime). ServiceChange must be the first message from a restarting MG; other commands must come afterward.

Responses must always be sent back to the source address of the request, even if the ServiceChangeAddress parameter specifies a different address for subsequent requests. This rule prevents commands and responses from being packed together improperly.
sections.eli5: Messages go over TCP or UDP to ports 2944 (text) or 2945 (binary). When a gateway starts up, it picks a random wait time, then tells its main controller 'I'm here', or tries the backup controllers if the main one doesn't answer.

sections.title: Security: Protecting Protocol and Media
sections.content:
The protocol defines two levels of security: protection of the protocol connection itself and protection of the media streams being carried.

Protocol Connection Security uses IPsec where the operating system and network support it. For IPv4 systems where IPsec is not available, the protocol defines an interim Authentication Header (AH) scheme. This optional header, placed within the Megaco protocol header, provides integrity checking using a synthesized IP pseudo-header (32-bit source and destination addresses plus UDP or TCP port) and manual keys following RFC 2402. The interim AH scheme does not protect against eavesdropping or replay attacks, but it identifies misbehaving entities. IPv6 implementations are assumed to support IPsec and must not use the interim scheme.

Media Connection Security protects the actual voice and video streams. The protocol allows the MGC to provide session keys to the MG for encryption. A basic protection is to accept media packets only from the announced source address and port (Remote Descriptor), but this can be slow and spoofable. Encryption with a secret key conveyed during call setup is stronger, providing protection against address spoofing without slowing call establishment.
sections.eli5: To protect the control messages between controller and gateway, the protocol can use IPsec or a simpler authentication header. To protect the actual phone calls, the controller can give the gateway a secret key to encrypt the audio.

sections.title: Gateway Control Interface and State Management
sections.content:
The MGC-MG relationship is initiated by the MG announcing itself via ServiceChange and is managed through subsequent state transitions.

Registration happens when an MG sends a ServiceChange with Restart method on the Root Termination. The MGC responds, and the MG and MGC establish a control association. The MG may propose a ServiceChangeAddress for the MGC to use; the MGC may also propose one in its reply. Either way, the recipient must use that address for all subsequent request transactions, though replies always return to the request source.

Protocol Version Negotiation occurs on the initial ServiceChange. The MG includes its supported protocol version. If the MGC supports a lower version, it replies with that lower version and both sides conform to it. If unable to agree, the MGC rejects with error 406 (Version Not Supported).

Multiple Virtual MGs allow a single physical gateway to partition its terminations among multiple MGCs. Physical terminations are assigned to one MGC, while ephemeral terminations (RTP flows) can be created per virtual MG. One MGC is designated the Master with read/write access to shared resources; others have read-only access. Each virtual MG has its own Root Termination.

Failure Handling: If an MG detects MGC failure, it attempts secondary MGCs in order. If it sends a ServiceChange with Graceful method and null delay, it stops accepting new connections but lets existing ones complete. Upon MGC failure, if the MG gets a ServiceChange from the MGC with HandOff method, it should contact the new MGC specified in ServiceChangeMgcId. The MG maintains termination and context state during handoff.

Package Definition is the primary extension mechanism. Packages define additional Properties, Events, Signals and Statistics for specific termination types. Packages are registered with IANA and should be documented in public standards or RFCs.
sections.eli5: When a gateway starts, it registers itself with the controller. If the controller fails, the gateway tries a backup. If the controller orders a handoff, the gateway switches to a new controller smoothly. Extensions are done by defining packages—named bundles of new features.

sections.title: Example: A Residential Gateway Call
sections.content: The RFC includes example call flows showing a two-gateway call. A residential gateway with two analog lines connects through the Megaco protocol to a Media Gateway Controller. The MGC sets up each gateway's terminations (the analog lines) by sending Add commands with media descriptors and events to detect (off-hook, digits). When a user picks up line 1 (off-hook), the MG sends a Notify with the event. The MGC responds with a signal (dial tone) applied via an embedded Signals descriptor in a Modify command. As digits arrive, the MG buffers and detects them; when a digit pattern completes (matching a digit map), it notifies the MGC. The MGC, having resolved the destination, moves the originating termination to a context with a remote termination (on the other gateway or network), applying media descriptors to set up RTP or other streams. Answer, speech, and disconnect follow similar patterns of Add, Modify, Subtract commands and Notify reports.
sections.eli5: When someone picks up a phone, the gateway tells the controller. The controller sends back a dial tone. When the person dials, the gateway recognizes the digits and tells the controller. The controller connects the call to the other side. All of this is commands back and forth.
